explanation: Digital Platform Proficiency is the capability to use and guide teams in applying digital tools, metadata-enabled discovery platforms, dashboards, and automated screening systems to identify needs, assess data availability, and support continuous evaluation. In practice, it enables the Unit Head to move from ad hoc reviews to standardized, digitally enabled workflows that scan data assets, triage requests by cost, impact, reusability, and automation fit, and support evidence-based business cases for new collection only when necessary.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to continuous digital scanning, enterprise-wide prioritization, automation, and stronger use of existing data before launching new surveys. These change drivers directly reshape GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.5, and 8.2 by requiring digitally enabled needs discovery, automated data suitability assessment, and dashboard-based real-time evaluation, making digital platform proficiency essential for future operational leadership.

explanation: Business case development is the capability to build clear, evidence-based cases for new data collections by assessing existing data options first and documenting cost-benefit, risk, resource needs, and automation fit. In the future workflow, this supports continuous digital needs scanning, standardized triage, and faster governance decisions by ensuring proposals are aligned with enterprise platforms, reusable data sources, and scalable automated approaches.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward faster, more transparent, and digitally enabled decision-making, with stronger expectations for reuse of existing data, automation, and enterprise alignment. These change drivers directly reshape GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 by requiring staff to formally identify needs through digital discovery, exhaustively assess data availability and suitability before proposing new collection, and prepare business cases that clearly justify trade-offs, resource use, and strategic fit.

explanation: Digital Stakeholder Engagement is the capability to use digital platforms, metadata tools, dashboards, and structured consultation methods to identify needs, assess feasibility, and synthesize stakeholder input into clear enterprise priorities. It supports a shift from ad hoc consultations to continuous, digitally enabled scanning, where staff guide stakeholders through trade-offs on reuse, cost, impact, timeliness, and automation fit while documenting decisions for agile review and downstream workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 8.2 requires earlier, more formalized stakeholder engagement and feasibility analysis through searchable metadata platforms, AI-supported discovery, and continuous evaluation dashboards. It is driven by the direction set out in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital service delivery, greater reuse of existing data, stronger prioritization discipline, and faster, evidence-based decision-making that directly reshape how needs are identified, confirmed, and evaluated.

explanation: This capability is the ability to identify needs using digital and AI-enabled approaches, assess existing data and automation options before proposing new collection, and apply cross-program resource optimization when setting priorities. It includes using standardized tools, metadata-driven discovery, and cost-benefit triage to build defensible business cases, while designing needs identification in ways that support reusable, auditable, and automation-ready downstream processes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to continuous digital scanning, stronger use of administrative and alternative data, and more efficient enterprise-wide allocation of resources. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5, these change drivers shift work toward automated data discovery, evidence-based justification for new surveys, and modular automation-ready design, making digital/AI readiness and resource optimization essential for meeting future operational requirements.

explanation: Continuous Digital Assessment is the capability to use digital tools, metadata, and standardized operational frameworks to continuously review whether programs, data sources, and processes remain feasible, sustainable, and ready for automation or AI. It supports earlier triage of needs, systematic checking of data availability and suitability, and faster action planning by embedding ongoing capacity monitoring, evidence-based decision-making, and enterprise-wide alignment into routine work.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, integrated, and responsive ways of working, where decisions must be supported by automation, enterprise prioritization, and stronger stewardship of resources. These change drivers shift work from periodic manual reviews to continuous digital scanning and triage across identifying needs, assessing data suitability, and agreeing action plans, making this capability essential for future operational readiness.

explanation: Automation Compatibility Analysis is the capability to evaluate whether program requirements, data sources, and business rules can be designed for automation, AI/ML use, and digital workflows from the outset. It includes assessing automation readiness, using metadata and standardized decision frameworks, and translating requirements into modular, machine-actionable, auditable processes that support reuse, interoperability, and faster operational delivery.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point to greater use of digital, automation, and AI-enabled operating models, which directly changes how needs are identified, data suitability is assessed, and processing is designed. These drivers require staff to formally integrate automation compatibility, enterprise triage, FAIR-based metadata practices, and standardized reusable workflows into decision-making, especially across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5, where future work depends on machine-actionable, scalable, and audit-ready design choices.

explanation: Digital Transformation Leadership is the capability to guide teams in adopting digital, solution-first ways of working by evaluating options through cost, risk, resource, and reusability lenses, and by building strong business cases for change. In practice, this means leading staff to use enterprise tools, metadata-enabled platforms, and automation-ready processes when identifying needs, designing outputs, and managing dissemination, while building team confidence in digital platforms and AI-ready workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to a sustained digital transition, stronger enterprise prioritization, and greater use of automation, interoperable platforms, and AI-enabled processes. These change drivers directly influence future requirements across GSBPM 1.1, 2.1, and 7.3, where leaders must ensure teams prioritize existing data and digital solutions first, develop defensible business cases for new collection or dissemination approaches, and operationalize digital/AI readiness through standardized, auditable, and platform-based workflows.

explanation: Data Discovery Platform Navigation is the capability to use approved data discovery and metadata tools to quickly identify existing data assets, assess their suitability, and support needs discussions with stakeholders. In future work across identifying, confirming, and checking data needs, employees must navigate these platforms to enable faster, evidence-based decisions, promote reuse of existing resources, and document trade-offs transparently before proposing new collection.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 requires staff to use standardized discovery platforms, machine-actionable metadata, and rapid asset evaluation processes that are not reflected in the current activity description. It is driven by the direction set in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital enablement, reuse of existing data, stronger prioritization, automation compatibility, and more transparent, enterprise-wide decision-making for new data requests.

explanation: Agile Stakeholder Engagement is the ability to lead short, structured, evidence-based discussions with stakeholders to confirm needs using data discovery tools, machine-actionable metadata, and clear prioritization criteria. It requires staff to quickly assess whether existing data assets can meet needs, make trade-offs transparent, and guide decisions on reuse, feasibility, timeliness, and resource alignment before proposing new collection activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to faster, more digital, reuse-first, and evidence-driven ways of working. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5, these change drivers increase the need for employees to facilitate rapid iterative consultations, use metadata and AI-enabled discovery platforms, and support transparent cost-benefit and prioritization discussions that determine whether needs can be met through existing assets or require justified new collection.

explanation: Transparent Criteria Application is the capability to use clear, consistent, and outcome-driven criteria when assessing stakeholder needs and recommending whether to reuse existing data, pursue alternative sources, or propose new collection. In future work across identifying needs, consulting with stakeholders, and checking data availability, employees will need to use data discovery platforms, metadata, and documented trade-off analysis to assess feasibility, resource alignment, timeliness, impact, and cost-benefit in a transparent and auditable way.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future state described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more disciplined, transparent, and evidence-based decision-making on whether new statistical activities should proceed. The change drivers emphasize digital service delivery, reuse of existing data assets, stronger prioritization, and responsible resource stewardship, which directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to apply explicit agency criteria, document trade-offs, and justify recommendations through feasibility, impact, and cost-benefit analysis.

explanation: Agency Asset Inventory Awareness is the capability to quickly identify, interpret, and use the agency’s data holdings, metadata repositories, and discovery platforms to assess whether existing sources can meet a need before new collection is considered. In future work across identifying, checking, and confirming needs, employees must use standardized inventories, machine-actionable metadata, and platform-based evidence to support rapid feasibility assessments, transparent prioritization, and well-documented decisions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts early-phase statistical work toward automated data discovery, metadata-assisted needs triage, and evidence-based decisions on reuse before launching new surveys. It is also reinforced by Mandate letters that emphasize efficient, transparent, and responsive use of public resources, making real-time awareness of agency assets essential for meeting stricter feasibility, prioritization, and resource-alignment requirements.

explanation: Advanced Articulation of Trade-offs is the capability to clearly explain evidence-based options, constraints, and consequences so stakeholders can make informed decisions aligned with agency priorities. In future work across needs confirmation, output design, and interpretation of results, employees will need to use platform evidence, metadata, dashboards, and AI-supported outputs to frame recommendations against feasibility, timeliness, reuse, quality, and resource considerations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future state described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more transparent prioritization, faster platform-enabled consultation, and greater reliance on reusable data assets and AI-supported workflows. These change drivers increase the need for employees in GSBPM 1.2, 2.1, and 6.3 to synthesize evidence from discovery platforms and automated outputs, communicate cost-benefit and impact trade-offs, and justify resource-informed recommendations in multi-stakeholder settings.

explanation: Real-time feasibility assessment is the capability to quickly determine whether a data need can be met using existing internal, administrative, or alternative data before recommending any new collection or program change. It requires staff to use standardized criteria, metadata-enabled discovery tools, and resource, risk, and suitability checks to support transparent, evidence-based decisions across need identification, consultation, and data availability assessment.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 requires staff to justify new surveys only after platform-enabled review confirms that existing assets are insufficient, while also documenting cost, impact, reusability, feasibility, and strategic fit. This aligns with the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively push the organization toward digital-first, efficient, transparent, and asset-centric operations where recommendations must be supported by real-time evidence and resource alignment.

explanation: Outcome-driven prioritization logic is the capability to make and document decisions using clear criteria tied to agency outcomes, cost-benefit, feasibility, and resource trade-offs. In practice, it enables staff to assess existing assets, confirm whether needs can be met through reuse, and develop action plans and output objectives that are transparent, traceable, and aligned with automation, timeliness, and enterprise priorities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.2, 1.3, and 8.3 requires staff to apply explicit prioritization criteria when confirming needs, setting output objectives, and agreeing action plans, rather than relying on broad improvement proposals. This is directly influenced by the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which emphasize modernization, reuse of existing data assets, digital and automated workflows, stronger accountability, and faster evidence-based decisions grounded in transparent trade-offs and measurable outcomes.

explanation: Enterprise Data Asset Evaluation is the capability to systematically identify, assess, and prioritize internal, administrative, alternative, and external data assets before proposing new collection. It requires staff to use repository and metadata systems, apply governance, legal, privacy, quality, interoperability, and automation-readiness criteria, and support objective-setting with evidence that existing assets can meet needs through scalable digital workflows. This capability is especially critical in GSBPM 1.1, 1.3, and 1.5, where needs, output objectives, and data suitability assessments must increasingly be automated, exhaustive, and survey-last by design.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires programs to default to reuse of enterprise data assets, administrative and alternative data, and automation-enabled delivery before considering manual or survey-based approaches. The change to work directly shifts GSBPM 1.1, 1.3, and 1.5 toward automated discovery, suitability screening, interoperability standards, and evidence-based justification for new collection, while the current state remains focused on statistical content without systematic evaluation of digital, reusable, and automation-ready options.

explanation: Automation Feasibility Assessment is the capability to systematically evaluate whether a data need can be met through existing data assets, administrative or alternative sources, or automated and digital workflows before proposing manual or survey-based approaches. It includes assessing automation readiness, interoperability, risk, cost, and suitability, and documenting clear evidence when manual collection is still required across needs identification, output objective setting, and data availability assessment.
justification: This skill gap was selected because current work on determining standards and techniques does not sufficiently assess digital integration or automation feasibility, while future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.3, and 1.5 requires explicit, evidence-based triage of automation, reuse, and survey necessity. This direction is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-first service delivery, enterprise data reuse, interoperability, and automation-enabled decision-making, thereby making objective automation assessment essential to future work requirements.

explanation: Interoperability standards capability means understanding and applying the data, metadata, process, and technical standards that allow statistical programs, systems, and outputs to work together seamlessly. In practice, this supports setting output objectives that are automation-enabled and machine-readable, checking data availability through standardized metadata, and integrating survey, administrative, and alternative data through reusable, auditable pipelines with minimal manual intervention.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward more digital, integrated, reusable, and efficient statistical production. Those drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.3, 1.5, and 5.1 by requiring output objectives to meet interoperability and automation criteria, data discovery to rely on machine-actionable metadata and FAIR-aligned standards, and data integration to occur through standardized, modular architectures rather than manual, program-specific processes.

explanation: This capability is the ability to assess program options using a structured cost/benefit lens that also tests digital feasibility, automation readiness, reuse potential, and respondent burden. In practice, it supports needs identification, data availability assessment, and evaluation activities by requiring staff to compare alternatives systematically, document trade-offs, and align recommendations with dashboard-driven monitoring, standardized decision rules, and digital execution requirements.
justification: This skill gap was selected because current recommendations do not consistently apply digital execution alignment or automation-readiness criteria, which is no longer sufficient under the future-state expectations set by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide. Those change drivers point to more digitally enabled, reuse-first, and continuously evaluated operations, so future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 8.2 requires explicit cost/benefit analysis, documented automation trade-offs, and evidence that proposed options fit enterprise digital guardrails and system-driven decision processes.

explanation: This capability is the ability to formally document why a methodological option was chosen, what alternatives were considered, and the trade-offs involved, especially when proposing new survey investments. In future work across identifying needs, checking data availability, and preparing business cases, staff must produce clear, evidence-based justification that shows existing data, administrative or alternative sources, automation opportunities, respondent burden, cost-benefit, and digital execution alignment were systematically assessed before recommending collection.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state requirements described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shift work toward reuse-first, digitally enabled, and automation-compatible decision-making, while Mandate letters reinforce expectations for efficient, transparent, and lower-burden public service delivery. These change drivers directly influence activities 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 by requiring explicit, auditable justification of why non-survey options were insufficient, how cost, risk, and sustainability were weighed, and why any proposed survey or manual approach is necessary.

explanation: Cross-Functional Digital Collaboration is the ability to work from project outset with IT, automation, and workflow specialists to design statistical processes that are modular, interoperable, and automation-ready. It includes coordinating technical and business stakeholders, translating program needs into machine-actionable workflow requirements, and supporting shared responsibility for auditable, metadata-driven pipelines across design, integration, and production activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in StatCan 2030 Future Slide for GSBPM 2.5, 2.6, and 5.1 requires statistical teams to collaborate early and continuously with IT, data engineering, and automation specialists to build standardized, reusable, and governed digital workflows. It is also driven by the Mandate letters and Departmental Plan emphasis on digital modernization, interoperability, responsible automation, and enterprise approaches, which together shift work from statistically scoped project design toward integrated delivery models where technical stakeholder management and cross-functional collaboration are essential.

explanation: Metadata-Driven Concept Systems is the capability to understand and apply metadata structures, repositories, and interoperability protocols so staff can validate, arbitrate, and govern AI-suggested concepts, data assets, and processing designs. As concept identification, data suitability assessment, and processing design become more automated across GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 2.5, employees must ensure proposed concepts align with standards, FAIR principles, and downstream system integration requirements while managing exceptions and cross-program conflicts.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to greater automation, interoperability, reuse of data assets, and AI-enabled decision support across the statistical production process. Those change drivers shift work away from manual concept development toward validating machine-generated recommendations, justifying departures from automated suggestions, and ensuring metadata-driven, auditable, and interoperable decisions for rapid, end-to-end digital operations.

explanation: This capability is the ability to review, compare, and adjudicate between multiple AI- or machine-suggested concept definitions and system outputs, making defensible exception decisions when standard options do not fully meet program needs. It shifts work away from manually creating concepts toward validating automated suggestions, resolving conflicts across programs, and ensuring decisions support interoperability, FAIR metadata principles, auditability, and sector-specific requirements in fast, metadata-driven workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to greater standardization, interoperability, automation, and trusted use of AI across statistical production. These drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.4, 2.6, and 6.3 by making automated concept identification, reusable production systems, and AI-supported interpretation the norm, which increases the need for staff who can arbitrate between machine-generated options, justify deviations from standards, and balance enterprise harmonization with sectoral needs.

explanation: This capability is the ability to clearly document when and why teams depart from proposed digital standards, especially in automated, modular, and interoperable workflows. It ensures exceptions are traceable, auditable, version controlled, and understandable across business, technical, and governance teams, so configurable rules, dissemination components, and edit/impute decisions can operate safely within approved guardrails.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and Statcan 2030 Future Slide points to more automated, AI-enabled, interoperable, and metadata-driven operations, where exceptions to standards must be explicitly justified and governed. Across GSBPM 2.5, 3.3, and 5.4, the shift toward reusable platforms, machine-actionable design, and auditable automated decision-making increases the need for staff to document exception rationale in ways that support compliance, explainability, cross-program consistency, and responsible digital governance.

explanation: Interoperability Impact Analysis is the ability to evaluate how AI-suggested, standardized concepts and automated data integration choices affect statistical findings, comparability, and the recommendations provided to sectors and programs. As concept identification, data suitability assessment, and integration become more automated under FAIR, metadata-driven processes, staff must interpret digital traceability, validate harmonization decisions, and clearly explain their downstream analytical impacts.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive greater standardization, interoperability, transparency, and automation across statistical production. These change drivers influence future work in GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 5.1 by requiring staff to work with AI-enabled concept discovery, automated suitability screening, and interoperable integration pipelines, making it essential to understand and communicate how machine-based harmonization affects findings, comparability, and evidence-based recommendations.

explanation: Automated Workflow Leadership is the capability to lead teams operating in machine-human hybrid environments where workflows are increasingly modular, automated, version-controlled, and auditable. It includes coordinating business and IT roles, managing conflicts arising from automated outputs and AI-supported decisions, and ensuring workflows remain transparent, standardized, and aligned with enterprise guardrails for quality, bias mitigation, and harmonization.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to future work that is more automated, interoperable, and governed through standardized enterprise platforms. Across GSBPM 3.4, 2.6, and 2.5, these change drivers increase the need for leaders who can manage machine-human workflow design and configuration, negotiate cross-program harmonization, and guide change in AI-enabled operations while maintaining accountability, auditability, and responsible use of automation.

explanation: Technical Mediation and Translation is the capability to interpret AI-generated harmonization decisions, explain exceptions and system conflicts, and communicate standards choices clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences. As processing, analysis, and dissemination become more automated, metadata-driven, and reusable, employees must turn complex machine logic into accessible, trustworthy explanations that support oversight, decision-making, and public understanding.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of AI, automation, standardized workflows, and machine-actionable outputs, which increases the need to explain how automated decisions are made and when exceptions apply. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 6.3, 2.5, and 2.1 by requiring staff to justify AI-supported outputs, arbitrate conflicts in automated rules and standards, and communicate methodological, ethical, and operational implications across diverse stakeholder groups.

skill_gap: Knowledge of Automated Suitability Assessment Systems
explanation: This capability is the ability to understand how automated suitability assessment and validation systems produce their results, and to judge whether those outputs are credible, complete, and appropriate for use or publication. As work shifts from manual analysis to monitoring automated discovery, validation, and interpretation processes across GSBPM 1.5, 6.2, and 6.3, staff must be able to review system-generated assessments, investigate exceptions, and clearly communicate quality, methodological, and ethical limitations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of automation, AI-enabled decision support, trusted data stewardship, and faster delivery of high-quality insights. Those change drivers directly influence future work requirements by making automated suitability screening, validation, and interpretation central to operations, which means employees must be able to oversee automated outputs, assess their reliability and fairness, and support transparent publication and decision-making.

explanation: This capability is the ability to use automated suitability and data discovery tools to assess whether existing data sources can meet a need, interpret the results, and decide on next steps. It requires staff to move from manually searching for options to reviewing machine-generated recommendations, validating their limits, documenting decisions, and balancing technical evidence with stakeholder, legal, privacy, and operational considerations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward more digital, efficient, and reuse-first ways of working, where new collection is justified only after existing data and automated options have been systematically assessed. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to use automated discovery and suitability tools, support formalized digital consultation, and make transparent, evidence-based decisions that align with sustainability, automation compatibility, and enterprise priorities.

skill_gap: Interpretation of Automated Data Source Rankings
explanation: This capability is the ability to interpret, explain, and defend program decisions using automated data source suitability rankings and AI-supported analytical outputs. As work shifts away from manually researching new sources, staff must apply judgment to assess automated recommendations, communicate their quality and limitations, and translate metadata-driven evidence into clear, decision-ready advice.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the StatCan 2030 Future Slide for GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 6.3 shifts source assessment, processing design, and analysis toward automated, metadata-driven, and AI-enabled workflows that still require strong human interpretation and oversight. It is also reinforced by the Departmental Plan and Mandate letters, which drive expectations for faster, evidence-based, transparent, and responsible decision making using modernized data and digital tools, increasing the need for leaders to interpret automated suitability reports and justify recommendations based on validated system outputs and partnership analysis.

explanation: Ecosystem Management Leadership is the capability to build and lead multidisciplinary teams that manage external partnerships, oversee legal and ethical review, curate high-quality machine-actionable metadata, and support automated assessment and dissemination processes. As work shifts from manual research and release tasks toward automated data discovery, governed dissemination, and AI-enabled promotion, leaders must organize teams around relationship management, metadata quality, validation, and exception handling across legal, privacy, technical, and program functions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.5, 7.3, and 7.4 requires Unit Heads to recruit and lead teams focused on metadata curation, automated suitability and release validation, and partnership management rather than primarily manual research and release activities. This direction is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize modernization, responsible automation, interoperable data and dissemination systems, and stronger collaboration with external data partners—thereby increasing the need for leadership that can coordinate ecosystem operations across legal, privacy, technical, and business domains.
